particle-decisions.title: Read the particle story
particle-decisions.intro: Switch between scenarios about particles, physical separation and temperature. Predict first, then check your reasoning.

questions.name: One type of molecule
questions.prompt: A sample contains only identical molecules, each made from two atoms of X bonded to one atom of Y. X and Y are different elements. How is the sample classified?
questions.explanation: There is one chemical substance containing two elements in a fixed ratio. Multiple elements in each molecule do not make the sample a mixture.

questions.name: Recover the solvent
questions.prompt: A non-volatile solid is dissolved in water. Which method collects the water as a liquid?
questions.explanation: The water vaporizes and is condensed into a separate container. Filtration does not remove a dissolved solute; evaporation to dryness does not collect the solvent.

questions.name: Temperature scale
questions.prompt: A fictional sample is at 26.85 °C. Convert this temperature to kelvin using T / K = temperature / °C + 273.15.
questions.explanation: 26.85 + 273.15 = 300.00 K. Temperature in kelvin is proportional to the average kinetic energy in the ideal-gas model.

questions.name: Melting plateau
questions.prompt: A pure solid melts at constant pressure. During the melting plateau, what happens as energy is supplied?
options: Average kinetic energy stays approximately constant while potential energy increases
questions.answer: Average kinetic energy stays approximately constant while potential energy increases
questions.explanation: Energy overcomes attractions as the solid becomes liquid. The temperature remains constant during the phase change; particles continue moving.

periodic-patterns.title: Explain a periodic pattern
periodic-patterns.intro: Compare positions and electron arrangements. Use shielding, occupied shells and nuclear charge to explain a trend rather than memorizing an arrow.

questions.name: Across period 3
questions.prompt: Which atom is generally smaller: sodium or chlorine?
questions.explanation: Across period 3 the nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same main shell. Similar shielding and greater attraction generally decrease atomic radius.

questions.name: Down group 1
questions.prompt: Which requires less energy to remove its first electron as a gaseous atom: lithium or potassium?
questions.explanation: Potassium's outer electron is in a more distant shell and is more shielded. These effects outweigh its larger nuclear charge.

questions.name: Read the arrangement
questions.prompt: A neutral main-group atom has electron arrangement 2,8,7. In which group and period is it found?
questions.explanation: Three occupied main shells indicate period 3. Seven outer-shell electrons place this main-group element in group 17.

functional-groups.title: Spot the functional group
functional-groups.intro: Read condensed structural formulas and distinguish groups that contain similar atoms but different bonding arrangements.

questions.name: CH₃CH₂OH
questions.prompt: Which class contains CH₃CH₂OH?
questions.explanation: The hydroxyl group is attached to a saturated carbon. There is no carbonyl group and the oxygen is not bonded to two carbon groups.

questions.name: CH₃COOCH₃
questions.prompt: Which class contains CH₃C(=O)OCH₃?
questions.explanation: An ester contains –C(=O)–O– between carbon-containing groups. A carboxylic acid would have –C(=O)–OH.

questions.name: CH₃COCH₃
questions.prompt: Which class contains CH₃C(=O)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups. An aldehyde has a hydrogen directly attached to its carbonyl carbon.

questions.name: Homologous series
questions.prompt: What is the formula difference between successive members of the same unbranched saturated alcohol homologous series?
questions.explanation: Successive members differ by CH₂ and retain the same functional group. Their physical properties show trends, while many chemical properties are similar.

calorimetry.title: Follow the heat in a calorimeter
calorimetry.intro: Use fictional measurements and q = mcΔT. Assume no heat loss and neglect the heat capacity of the container. The solution and reaction have opposite heat signs.

questions.name: Heat gained by solution
questions.prompt: 100.0 g of solution warms by 5.00 K. Use c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the heat gained by the solution in kJ.
questions.explanation: q = 100.0 × 4.18 × 5.00 = 2090 J = +2.09 kJ. The reaction releases this heat.

questions.name: Molar reaction enthalpy
questions.prompt: A reaction involving 0.0500 mol of the limiting reactant transfers 2.09 kJ to its surroundings. Find ΔH per mole of that reactant.
questions.explanation: q(reaction) = −2.09 kJ, so ΔH = −2.09 / 0.0500 = −41.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Heat release is exothermic.

questions.name: Cooling solution
questions.prompt: The solution cools during a reaction in an insulated calorimeter. What is the sign of the reaction enthalpy?
questions.explanation: The reaction absorbs heat from the solution. The solution loses thermal energy while the reacting system gains it.

energy-cycles.title: Choose a path through an energy cycle
energy-cycles.intro: Practise Hess’s law with invented thermochemical data. Reverse an equation and its enthalpy sign together; scale both by the same factor.

questions.name: Add two steps
questions.prompt: For fictional states A, B and C: A → B has ΔH = +45 kJ mol⁻¹ and B → C has ΔH = −120 kJ mol⁻¹. Find ΔH for A → C.
questions.explanation: Add the steps: +45 + (−120) = −75 kJ mol⁻¹. B cancels from the overall change.

questions.name: Reverse a step
questions.prompt: A → C has ΔH = −75 kJ mol⁻¹. Find ΔH for C → A.
questions.explanation: Reversing the chemical change reverses the enthalpy sign: +75 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.name: Bond enthalpy estimate
questions.prompt: For one mole of a fictional gas-phase reaction, breaking bonds requires 680 kJ and forming bonds releases 850 kJ. Estimate ΔH.
questions.explanation: ΔH ≈ sum of bond enthalpies broken − sum formed = 680 − 850 = −170 kJ mol⁻¹. Bond breaking requires energy; bond formation releases energy.

fuel-energy.title: Compare useful energy from fuels
fuel-energy.intro: Use supplied fictional fuel data to compare energy per mass and useful output. Keep energy released as a positive quantity here, unlike a negative combustion enthalpy.

questions.name: Energy per gram
questions.prompt: Fuel X has molar mass 40.0 g mol⁻¹ and releases 1600 kJ mol⁻¹ on complete combustion. How much energy is released per gram?
questions.explanation: 1600 / 40.0 = 40.0 kJ g⁻¹. Energy per mole alone is not enough to compare equal masses of fuels.

questions.name: Useful energy
questions.prompt: Burning 2.00 g of fuel X releases 40.0 kJ g⁻¹. A device transfers 30.0% of this energy to its intended use. Calculate the useful energy.
questions.explanation: Total energy = 2.00 × 40.0 = 80.0 kJ. Useful energy = 80.0 × 0.300 = 24.0 kJ.

questions.name: Limited oxygen
questions.prompt: Why can burning a hydrocarbon with insufficient oxygen be dangerous?
options: It can form toxic carbon monoxide
questions.answer: It can form toxic carbon monoxide
questions.explanation: Incomplete combustion may form carbon monoxide and soot rather than converting all carbon to carbon dioxide.

gibbs-energy.title: Find the temperature boundary (AHL)
gibbs-energy.intro: For fictional data use ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°. Convert entropy from J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Assume ΔH° and ΔS° are constant over the temperature range.

questions.name: At 300 K
questions.prompt: ΔH° = +40.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG° at 300 K.
questions.explanation: ΔS° = 0.100 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG° = 40.0 − 300 × 0.100 = +10.0 kJ mol⁻¹. The forward change is not spontaneous under standard-state conditions at this temperature.

questions.name: Boundary temperature
questions.prompt: With ΔH° = +40.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, at what temperature is ΔG° = 0?
questions.explanation: T = ΔH° / ΔS° = 40.0 / 0.100 = 400 K. Above this temperature ΔG° is negative within this constant-data approximation.

questions.name: Thermodynamics versus speed
questions.prompt: A reaction has negative ΔG under the stated conditions. What can you conclude?
options: It is thermodynamically spontaneous but may be slow
Its activation energy must be zero
questions.answer: It is thermodynamically spontaneous but may be slow
questions.explanation: The Gibbs energy change describes thermodynamic direction. A large activation barrier can make a spontaneous change very slow.

reaction-rates.title: Read rate evidence
reaction-rates.intro: Use invented measurements to calculate an average rate, then distinguish a faster pathway from a different final equilibrium.

questions.name: Average rate
questions.prompt: A reactant concentration decreases from 0.80 to 0.50 mol dm⁻³ over 60.0 s. Calculate its positive average rate of disappearance.
questions.explanation: Rate of disappearance = −Δ[reactant]/Δt = (0.80 − 0.50)/60.0 = 0.0050 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. This is an interval average, not an instantaneous rate.

questions.name: Catalyst
questions.prompt: At the same temperature, what does a catalyst change?
options: It provides a pathway with lower activation energy
questions.answer: It provides a pathway with lower activation energy
questions.explanation: A catalyst increases forward and reverse rates without changing ΔH or the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature.

questions.name: Surface area
questions.prompt: Equal masses of a solid react with identical excess acid under otherwise identical conditions. Which usually gives the greater initial rate?
options: Both must have the same initial rate
questions.explanation: The powder exposes more surface for collisions with the acid. Equal mass does not imply equal exposed surface area.

proton-transfer.title: Track a proton
proton-transfer.intro: Identify Brønsted–Lowry roles and conjugate pairs, then calculate pH for a supplied ideal dilute solution.

questions.name: Identify the base
questions.prompt: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which reactant accepts a proton?
questions.explanation: NH₃ accepts H⁺ to form NH₄⁺ and acts as a base. Water donates H⁺ in this reaction and acts as an acid.

questions.name: Conjugate pair
questions.prompt: Which pair differs by exactly one proton?
questions.explanation: A conjugate acid–base pair differs by one H⁺. The other pairs differ by two protons.

questions.name: Calculate pH
questions.prompt: An ideal dilute solution has [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Use pH = −log₁₀[H⁺].
questions.explanation: −log₁₀(0.00100) = 3.00. A tenfold decrease in [H⁺] would increase pH by one.

electron-transfer.title: Account for transferred electrons
electron-transfer.intro: Use oxidation states and half-equations to identify oxidation, reduction and the role of an oxidizing agent.

questions.name: Oxidation state
questions.prompt: In MnO₄⁻, each oxygen has oxidation state −2. What is the oxidation state of manganese?
questions.explanation: Let x be the Mn oxidation state: x + 4(−2) = −1, so x = +7.

questions.name: Electron count
questions.prompt: How many electrons are released when one Zn atom forms Zn²⁺?
questions.explanation: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Loss of electrons is oxidation; charge is conserved.

questions.name: Oxidizing agent
questions.prompt: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Which species is the oxidizing agent?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ accepts electrons and is reduced. By accepting those electrons it causes zinc to be oxidized.

radical-steps.title: Sort a radical chain reaction
radical-steps.intro: Classify steps in the photochemical chlorination of methane. A dot denotes an unpaired electron; a radical is not the same as an ion.

questions.name: Cl₂ → 2Cl•
questions.prompt: UV light causes Cl₂ → 2Cl•. Which stage is this?
questions.explanation: Homolytic bond fission gives one bonding electron to each chlorine atom, creating two radicals.

questions.name: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•
questions.prompt: A chlorine radical removes a hydrogen atom from methane, producing a methyl radical. Which stage is this?
questions.explanation: One radical is consumed and another is formed, allowing the chain to continue. CH₃• can react with Cl₂ to form CH₃Cl and regenerate Cl•.

questions.name: CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl
questions.prompt: A methyl radical combines with a chlorine radical to form chloromethane. Which stage is this?
questions.explanation: Two radicals combine and no new radical is formed, ending that chain pathway.

electron-pairs.title: Follow the donated electron pair
electron-pairs.intro: Recognize electron-pair donors and acceptors and predict simple substitution and addition products. Distinguish a full electron pair from the single electrons in radical reactions.

questions.name: Nucleophile
questions.prompt: In CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻, which species donates the electron pair that forms the new C–O bond?
questions.explanation: Hydroxide donates a lone pair to the electrophilic carbon. The C–Br bond breaks and bromide leaves.

questions.name: Substitution product
questions.prompt: Bromoethane reacts with aqueous hydroxide by substitution. What organic product forms?
questions.explanation: The hydroxyl group replaces bromine on the carbon chain. The stated pathway is substitution, not elimination.

questions.name: Addition to ethene
questions.prompt: Hydrogen bromide adds across the C=C bond of ethene. Which product forms?
questions.explanation: H and Br add to the two carbons of the double bond. The carbon–carbon bond becomes single and no small molecule is eliminated.
